title: Broken Access Control

levels.beginner: Access control answers one question: is this user allowed to do this thing to this object? It breaks when the app forgets to ask — a normal user opening an admin page, or viewing someone else's record by changing an ID.
levels.intermediate: The classic patterns are insecure direct object references (predictable IDs with no ownership check), missing function-level checks (the button is hidden but the API endpoint is open), and privilege escalation through a parameter the user controls.
levels.advanced: Enforce authorisation on the server for every request, using the authenticated identity and the object's owner — never trust a hidden form field or a client-side check. Prefer deny-by-default: every endpoint starts closed and explicitly grants what a role may do. Test with two accounts: what user B can do to user A's data is the test that matters.

key_points: Check ownership on the server for every object access, not only in the UI.
Deny by default; grant explicitly per role and per action.
Never trust IDs, roles or permissions sent by the client.
Use unpredictable IDs where possible, but never rely on secrecy alone.
Audit access decisions — log denied attempts.

defensive_examples.title: Ownership check on the server (pattern)
defensive_examples.code:
# Every single-object read must do this:
obj = db.query(Note).filter(Note.id == note_id).first()
if obj is None or obj.user_id != current_user.id:
    raise HTTPException(404, "Not found")  # 404, not 403: do not leak existence
defensive_examples.explanation: Returning 404 for another user's object hides whether it exists at all, and the check happens server-side where the client cannot bypass it.

knowledge_check.question: A page hides the 'Delete' button from normal users, but the delete API endpoint works without any role check. What is wrong?
options: Authorisation must be enforced on the server; hiding UI is not a control
The API needs a faster database
Nothing — users cannot find hidden buttons
knowledge_check.explanation: Anyone can call an API directly. The server must check the caller's role on every request, regardless of what the UI shows.

knowledge_check.question: Why return 404 instead of 403 when a user requests another user's private object?
options: So an attacker cannot learn whether the object exists
Because 404 is the only valid code
knowledge_check.explanation: A 403 confirms the object exists but is forbidden; a 404 reveals nothing, which prevents probing for other users' data.
